name: White Hmong
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: White, Nathan M. 2021. The Hmong Language of North Queensland. PhD thesis, James Cook University, Cairns. 742 pp. DOI 10.25903/f5rd-s089. Open PDF:https://researchonline.jcu.edu.au/81550/1/JCU_81550_White_2021_thesis.pdf(downloaded via the Internet Archive 20250925112124id_). Describes White Hmong (Hmoob Dawb) and Green Mong (Moob Ntsuab/Lees) as spoken in North Queensland; a version of §§3.1-3.4 is published as White 2020 'Word in Hmong'. Secondary (concordant support): Whitelock, Doris. 1982 [1966-68]. White Hmong Language Lessons. Revised edition (Southeast Asian Refugee Studies Occasional Papers 2, series ed. Bruce T. Downing). Minneapolis: CURA, University of Minnesota. Open PDF:https://conservancy.umn.edu/handle/11299/207895.
catalog_locator: White 2021: §2.3 Tones, p. 59; §2.8 Pragmatic prominences, p. 70; §3.1 Phonological word, p. 79 and p. 80 (register dependence); exception passage §3.1.3 Cliticization, p. 88 (=os). page numbers are the running heads at the top of each page.
catalog_quote: Hmong has seven phonemic tones, which vary in realization according to whether they are affected by lexical tone melody alternation processes ... or tone leveling processes realized in fast, non-careful speech. [§2.3, p. 59] ... In contexts where new information is given or a word is relatively important in its context, a pragmatic prominence tends to be placed on the final syllable of a phonological word (though with the exception of certain enclitic clause-final markers such as =os ‘CFM:SOFT’ if present; see section 3.3 below). The syllable affected by this pragmatic prominence contains a vowel that resists phonetic reduction or other forms of compression, and may exhibit an expanded pitch range for the realization of the tone. [§2.8, p. 70] ... Given this bias toward monosyllables, identifying word-level features such as stress is less than straightforward, since if the vast majority of words in a clause are monosyllabic, and every word has lexical stress, there will be no meaningful contrast in lexical stress for most of that clause. ... 1) The presence of a stressed syllable when a pragmatic prominence is present; and 2) the ability to place pauses only after a syllable that may receive stress. [§3.1, p. 79] ... If a speaker slows down significantly and pronounces syllables carefully in a register where careful speech is required, the prominence and pause placement characterizing casual, moderate-rate speech disappear ... [p. 80]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: REDUPLICATION: This is a common feature of Hmong occuring mainly in verbs and verbal adjectives. Have you noticed that when your informant says the reduplicated words at his normal rate of utterance the first word "loses its shape" i.e. the quality of the vowel is shortened or almost lost completely. There is stress on the second word. The contour of the tone is also changed - the first word having a shorter contour and the second word usually long and drawn out and on a higher pitch than the basic tone. [p. 37] ... The apostrophe (') used at the beginning of a syllable in pronunciation drills indicates the position of stress. [p. iv]
new_statements.citation: Whitelock, Doris. 1982 [1966-68]. White Hmong Language Lessons. Revised edition (Southeast Asian Refugee Studies Occasional Papers 2, series ed. Bruce T. Downing). Minneapolis: Center for Urban and Regional Affairs, University of Minnesota.
new_statements.locator: Lesson 3.C (Review), note 'REDUPLICATION', p. 37 (p. 44); editor's foreword by Bruce T. Downing, p. iv (p. 5)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (134 pp., text, UMN Conservancy scan, 'This report is not copyrighted'). extracted text of p. 44 = printed p. 37 (page number '37' at foot) gives the REDUPLICATION note word for word as quoted, including the spelling 'occuring', 'There is stress on the second word', the tone-contour remark, the nasalization remark for 'ee'/'oo', and the drill items (koj tus nees loj loj li, koj tus dev me me li..). p. 5 = p. iv (Downing's 'A Note On This Edition', continuing from p. iii) has verbatim 'The apostrophe (') used at the beginning of a syllable in pronunciation drills indicates the position of stress.' A a full-text search for stress/accent the whole text for stress/accent/emphasis/promine…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is given: White Hmong words are monosyllabic and tonal, and the only stress statement is about reduplicated verbs/adjectives (loj loj 'very big', me me 'very small'), where the second copy carries the stress (longer, higher-pitched tone contour) and the first copy is reduced (vowel shortened, nasalization lost). the compilers stress apostrophe is used in the body only in English-based articulation drills.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; note that with nasalized vowels ee/oo the first (unstressed) copy loses its nasalization.
new_statements.domain_note: Reduplicative phrase (two-word expression) at normal speech rate; pedagogical description for learners, not a phonological analysis of the word. Language is monosyllabic and tonal (7 tones per the same source); no source opened states whether isolated monosyllables or compounds bear stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Whitelock's lessons represent White Hmong (Hmong Daw) as spoken in a mountain village in North Thailand, revised in Northern Laos (foreword p. iii) — the same variety as hmon1333. Niederer, Smalley, Golston & Yang and Garellek et al. also describe White Hmong (Thailand/Laos/US diaspora). The Lyman 1979 file is Green Mong / Mong Njua (different Glottolog languoid), included only as a related-variety check.

tone_statements.citation: Garellek, Marc & Esposito, Christina M. 2021 [print 2023]. Phonetics of White Hmong vowel and tonal contrasts. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53(1): 213-232. doi:10.1017/S0025100321000104
tone_statements.quote: Additionally, morphemes are obligatorily specified with one of eight tones, of which all but one are lexical; see Table 2. All tones except the falling-rising -d (214) tone are lexical; the falling-rising -d (214) tone is not productive, but is found on certain high-frequency words (typically deictic markers). This tone developed from a merger of two morphemes bearing the low-falling creaky -m (21) tone followed by the mid-rising -v (24) tone (Ratliff 1992). The falling tones with non-modal phonation appear to be consistently breathy or creaky (Esposito 2012, Garellek et al. 2013, Garellek, Keating & Esposito 2014).
tone_statements.locator: §1.3 'Tonal inventory and tone sandhi' with Table 2 'White Hmong tonal inventory', p. 215

tone_statements.citation: Esposito, Christina M. 2012. An acoustic and electroglottographic study of White Hmong tone and phonation. Journal of Phonetics 40(3): 466-476. doi:10.1016/j.wocn.2012.02.007
tone_statements.quote: The Hmong (Hmong-Mien) languages have a complex tonal system that includes changes in pitch as well as phonation. For example, White Hmong has seven phonemic tones, two of which are associated with non-modal phonation. The traditional tonal description¹ is: high, mid, low, high-falling, mid-rising, low-falling creaky and mid-low breathy. (There is also an eighth tone which is a syntactic variant of the low-falling creaky tone.) ... However, the traditional description of the -g tone as a mid-low tone is inaccurate; the -g tone is a falling tone ... the data here suggests that the -b tone is more accurately described as rising.
tone_statements.locator: p. 466 sec. 1 Introduction; continuation after '..' from p. 471 sec. 4.1
tone_statements.summary: Seven phonemic tones (an eighth is a syntactic variant of low-falling creaky -m); -m creaky, -g breathy; F0 of 32 speakers: -b rising (45) not 55, -g falling; -b, -m shortest; females merging -j/-g.

tone_statements.citation: Fulop, Sean A. & Chris Golston. 2008. Breathy and whispery voicing in White Hmong. Proceedings of Meetings on Acoustics 4: 060006 (10 pp.).
tone_statements.quote: White Hmong is a seven-tone language, contrasting five modal-voice tones with distinctive pitch contours plus two others in which the phonation qualities (breathy versus creaky) seem to be the most salient feature. Hmong tones: pɔ̀ pɔ pɔ́ pɔ̂ pɔ̌ pɔ̰ pɔ̤ In this study our focus is on the breathy tone compared with the falling modal tone, which is judged to have the most similar pitch contour.
tone_statements.locator: manuscript pp. 2-3, §2.1 White Hmong phonology (tone list on p. 2, last clause after Table II on p. 3)
tone_statements.summary: Seven tones: five modal tones with distinct pitch contours plus a breathy and a creaky tone; the falling tone is written [ɔ̀]. Acoustic measures are of phonation (breathy vs falling tone), not F0.

tone_statements.citation: Ratliff, Martha (1987). Tone Sandhi compounding in White Hmong. LTBA 10. pp. 71-105.
tone_statements.quote: Many words with high falling, low level, low checked, mid rising, and mid level tones (those words marked with -j , -s , -m , -v , and ∅) respectively) have alternate tonal realizations when they enter into a particularly close relationship with a preceding word which has either a high level or high falling tone (-b , -j ). ... It makes sense to retain the distinction between "basic tones" and "sandhi tones" since the sandhi tones represent a neutralization of the number of contrasts embodied in the basic tone inventory. In White Hmong there are seven basic tones (two of which never undergo tone sandhi), but only three sandhi tones.
tone_statements.locator: p. 71 sec. 2.1 and p. 100 sec. 3.2 point (4)
tone_statements.summary: Seven tones written with RPA final letters; sandhi after -b/-j: -j,-s,-m > -g, -v > unmarked, unmarked > -s. Pitch values credited to Sprigg/Downer and Chinese sources. At least 10 forms.

tone_statements.citation: Rialland, Annie. 2005. Phonological and phonetic aspects of whistled languages. Phonology 22(2): 237-271. doi:10.1017/S0952675705000552
tone_statements.quote: White Hmong is a tone language with seven tones : Tone 1 (level-high, 55), Tone 2 (level-mid 33), Tone 3 (level-low 22), Tone 4 (low glottalized 21?), Tone 5 (mid-rising 24), Tone 6 (high-falling 52), and Tone 7 (murmured falling 42). [...] A comparison of the whistled and spoken versions confirms that it is the tone melody of the spoken utterance, rather than its F2 movements, that is transposed in whistled speech. Thus, the H1 movements of whistled speech (bottom) follow the F0 contour of the spoken utterance (top) and bear no relation to F2 movements.

sources.note: Full acoustic study of the tone system from multi-speaker connected speech: eight tones of which seven are lexical (55/45 -b, 33 unmarked, 22 -s, 52 -j, 24 -v, low-falling creaky 21 -m, high-falling breathy 42/52 -g) plus the non-productive falling-rising 214 -d; breathy and creaky phonation are systematic on -g and -m; describes tone sandhi after -b/-j and revises several contour descriptions; finds little evidence of post-lexical intonational f0 targets.

tone.quote: Many words with high falling, low level, low checked, mid rising, and mid level tones (those words marked with -j , -s , -m , -v , and ∅) respectively) have alternate tonal realizations when they enter into a particularly close relationship with a preceding word which has either a high level or high falling tone (-b , -j ). ... It makes sense to retain the distinction between "basic tones" and "sandhi tones" since the sandhi tones represent a neutralization of the number of contrasts embodied in the basic tone inventory. In White Hmong there are seven basic tones (two of which never undergo tone sandhi), but only three sandhi tones.
